name: Hybrid Immunity and Prior Infection Effects
anchorClaim: Individuals with both prior SARS-CoV-2 infection and vaccination (hybrid immunity) show measurably higher protection against reinfection or severe disease compared to vaccination alone, as reported in observational and cohort studies of vaccine effectiveness.
plainQuestion: Having had a prior COVID-19 infection, on top of being vaccinated, gives extra protection against reinfection or severe disease compared to vaccination alone.
confidenceSummary: The Grade D is a caution about strength: only a couple of the studies are randomized trials, and a good share of the supporting evidence holds only under specific conditions, such as a particular age group or virus variant.

guide.whatScienceSays: DATOM looked at 18 studies that directly tested this claim. Of those, 16 (89%) support the idea that a prior COVID-19 infection on top of vaccination gives extra protection against reinfection or severe disease compared with vaccination alone; 2 (11%) point the other way. So most of the clear findings back the claim, which is what the "Supported" verdict below means. But the Grade D beside it matters just as much: the evidence base is limited, so this is the current direction of the evidence, not a settled, high-certainty result. Many more studies touched on the topic without testing this exact claim; they appear further down, tagged by what they looked at.
guide.howConfident:
DATOM gives this claim a confidence score of 31%, which falls in the "Preliminary" band. That is noticeably lower than the 44% of evidence that directly supports the claim, a 13 point gap worth pointing out directly.

Confidence is not just a vote count. It measures how strong and how consistent the evidence actually is, and on both counts, this evidence base is weaker than the 44% headline number suggests.

Only 2 of the 45 pieces of evidence are randomized controlled trials, the gold-standard study design for proving cause and effect. But both of those two studies list their sample size as "Not reported," so we cannot actually check how much statistical weight they carry. Separately, DATOM's own scoring flags 9 of the 45 pieces of evidence as too small a group to trust the result strongly.

The rest of the evidence is spread across 36 different research methods: cohort studies using blood tests, case-control studies, disease-spread models, and literature reviews. It comes from 28 different published sources and 11 different institutions. That is a wide variety of angles, but almost none of them repeat each other, so there is very little independent confirmation of any single result.

On top of that, 24 of the 45 pieces of evidence (53%), more than half, are extracted as text only, without the full original document attached. None of the 45 have their journal information on file either. That means more than half of this evidence base cannot be independently double-checked against the original document.

Put it together: a 44% support rate, built mostly on conditional findings, spread across many different methods, with more than half impossible to independently verify. That combination earns a "Preliminary" score, even though outright contradiction is rare, just 4%.
decisionSupport: The evidence leans supportive overall: 20 of the 45 pieces of evidence (44%) support added protection from hybrid immunity, versus just 2 (4%) that argue against it. The strongest example is a study of 101,941 people showing hybrid immunity cut reinfection risk by 26 to 36%. But DATOM's confidence score is well below that raw support number, at 31% ("Preliminary"), so treat the lean toward "yes" as a starting point, not a final answer.

Be cautious with the two randomized controlled trials in this set: both list their sample size as "Not reported." Randomized trials are normally the strongest kind of evidence, but here we cannot check how much statistical weight they actually carry.

More than half the evidence, 23 of 45 pieces of evidence (51%), only applies under specific conditions: a certain age group, a certain variant, or a certain time period. For example, a finding from a study of 56 dialysis patients (a group with weaker immune systems) should not be assumed to apply to healthy adults without checking whether it actually does.

Do not treat hybrid immunity as full protection. A study of 535 people in Salvador, Brazil found that the BQ.1* variant still infected 56% of the population, even though about 97% of people there already had prior infection and/or vaccination.

Before citing this in anything important, check the original sources yourself. 24 of the 45 pieces of evidence (53%) are missing their full original document, and none of the 45 have journal information on file, so the underlying study should be looked up directly rather than trusted from the extracted summary alone.
guide.faultLines:
Few Strong Trials at the Top: only 2 of the 45 pieces of evidence are randomized controlled trials, the design best suited to prove cause and effect, and both list their sample size as "Not reported." DATOM's own scoring separately flags 9 of the 45 as too small a group to trust strongly. The other 43 are spread across 36 different research methods, observational studies, computer models, and literature reviews, drawn from 28 different published sources and 11 different institutions. That variety is wide, but it means almost nothing gets independently repeated and confirmed.

Real Disagreement Isn't Settled: 23 of the 45 pieces of evidence (51%), a slim majority, only support the claim under specific conditions. That might mean a certain group of people (like dialysis patients or older adults), a certain variant (like BQ.1*), or a certain time window. So the headline 44% support number is not one clean, consistent effect. It is a patchwork of different findings for different groups that has never been fully explained or brought together into one clear picture. The 535 person study in Salvador, Brazil is a direct example. The BQ.1* variant still infected 56% of people there, despite 97% already having prior infection and/or vaccination. That has never been fully resolved against a simple "hybrid immunity protects you" story.

We Can't Always Check the Sources: 24 of the 45 pieces of evidence (53%), more than half, are text extractions without the full original document, and journal information is missing for all 45. On top of that, 25 of the 45 (56%) are dated 2026, which DATOM has confirmed is a real, recent publication date rather than a data entry error. That means most of this evidence is both hard to independently double check, and too new to have been reviewed, repeated, or cited much by other researchers yet.
